extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians and advanced students interested in additive number theory (Waring's problem) and analytic methods
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of Waring's problem and related additive-number-theory problems with definitions, historical results, and analytic methods (generating functions, singular series / circle method) used to prove existence and asymptotic formulae for representations by k-th powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of r(n) (number of representations)
rubrics_metrics.description: r(n) is the number of representations of n that satisfy the conditions of the additive problem (choice of summands, restrictions on order/distinctness, and fixed or unrestricted s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: r(n) is naturally studied via generating functions f(x)=sum r(n) x^n; choice of conventions (order/sign) affects the generating function but not the essential analytic approach. Example: for sums of kth powers the generating function is f(x)=1+2a1 x + 2a2 x^2 + ... with ai counting k-th powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of generating functions and Cauchy's theorem to extract coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent the counting function as coefficients of a power series (generating function) and apply Cauchy's Theorem to express r(n) as a contour integral around the unit circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the fundamental analytic approach to additive problems: r(n) is the coefficient of x^n in f(x), so r(n) = (1/2πi) ∮ f(x) x^{-n-1} dx. The difficulty is the behaviour of f(x) on the unit circle: for many additive problems the whole unit circle is singular, so contour deformation and detailed local analysis are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction of analytic weapons: power series vs Dirichlet series
rubrics_metrics.description: For additive problems the proper tool is power (generating) series; for multiplicative problems (primes/divisors) the right weapon is Dirichlet series (e.g. zeta-function).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hardy emphasizes that multiplication of primes is natural (multiplicative structure of Dirichlet series) while addition of ranks is natural for power series. Use the appropriate series type for the problem-class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of g(k) (uniform representation bound)
rubrics_metrics.description: g(k) is the least number m (if it exists) such that every integer n is the sum of at most m k-th powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: g(2)=4 and g(3)=9 are known; for general k existence proofs and upper bounds are the main objectives. g(k) is an exact, global 'worst-case' metric for representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of G(k) (asymptotic / almost-all representation bound)
rubrics_metrics.description: G(k) is the least number such that every sufficiently large integer is the sum of at most G(k) k-th powers (i.e., 'every member from a certain point onwards').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: G(k) is often more fundamental than g(k); existence of G(k) implies existence of g(k). Distinguish between the two when proving results: proving G(k) often suffices for Waring-type conclusions about large n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congruence obstructions / modular lower bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Use congruence classes to show lower bounds on the number of k-th powers needed (e.g., numbers congruent to 7 mod 8 cannot be sums of three squares; certain residues mod 9/16 obstruct small representations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These elementary modular arguments give unavoidable lower bounds for G(k) (and hence g(k)). They provide simple necessary conditions and show that some minimal numbers of summands are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic identity constructions to obtain upper bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct explicit algebraic identities (sums of kth powers expressed as sums of other kth powers) to derive concrete upper bounds for g(k) (e.g., Liouville, Maillet identities yielding bounds for g(4), g(3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such identities produce effective (though sometimes large) explicit bounds. Hilbert's and later refinements give existence but often are not effective; simple algebraic identities are constructive and give explicit numerical upper bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semi-transcendental / Hilbert existence proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Hilbert's general existence proof for g(k) uses integral-calculus methods (initially integrals over high-dimensional regions) and shows identities exist that imply boundedness, but the proof is essentially non-effective for explicit g(k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: View Hilbert's method as an existence proof: it proves g(k) exists but does not provide explicit, manageable identities or small numerical bounds. Later work simplified and made proofs elementary but still non-effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circle method: major arcs (rational points) vs minor arcs
rubrics_metrics.description: In the integral for the coefficient, isolate contributions from neighbourhoods of rational points p/q on the unit circle (the 'major arcs'), which dominate, and treat the rest (the 'minor arcs') as smaller contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hardy & Littlewood's insight: rational points with small denominators produce the largest 'singularities' (lights on the rail); their contributions can be approximated and summed. Success of the method depends on controlling minor-arc error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction and role of the singular series
rubrics_metrics.description: Define the singular series (an arithmetical series summing exponential sums over q and residues) which multiplies the singular integral to give the principal asymptotic term in the representation formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The singular series S(n) is central: the leading term in r_s,k(n) is C n^{s/k -1} times S(n). One must analyze convergence, oscillation, and positivity of S(n). Examples and explicit expressions (Gauss sums when k=2) are given in the lecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asymptotic formula structure and growth exponent
rubrics_metrics.description: For sufficiently large s (and under method hypotheses), the number of representations has an asymptotic form: main_term ≍ constant * n^{s/k - 1} * singular_series + error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine the exponent s/k -1 (coming from singular integral) and show the error term is of lower order. The positivity of the leading constant and S(n) (for s large enough) implies representations exist for large n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement: singular series positive and error smaller than main term
rubrics_metrics.description: To conclude that r(n)>0 for large n one needs (a) the singular series (or leading term) to be positive, and (b) the error term to be of strictly lower order so it cannot cancel the main term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hardy stresses that both conditions are necessary: positivity ensures the main asymptotic contributes mass, and controlling the error (e.g., error = O(n^{s/k -1 - delta})) guarantees positivity persists for large n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominance of few terms in the singular series
rubrics_metrics.description: The terms of the singular series diminish rapidly; only a few terms (those with small denominators q) are of real importance and are oscillatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice one computes only the leading few q-terms to approximate S(n); examples are given for k=2, k=3, k=4 where the first few cosines dominate the behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for new analytic 'light' beyond rational points (minor-arc treatment)
rubrics_metrics.description: For k>2 the rational-point (major-arc) beams are too narrow and leave dark regions; an additional source of analytic control (induced 'glow' of the rail) is necessary to illuminate minor arcs sufficiently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hardy & Littlewood introduce weaker but widespread contributions (singular integral / smoothing) to make minor arcs visible; this is the subtle technical heart of extending the method beyond k=2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of computational evidence and tabulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical computation (tables of minimal numbers of summands up to large bounds, partition tables) is valuable for testing conjectures about g(k), G(k), and the distribution of exceptional n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hardy cites extensive tables (e.g., up to 40,000 for cubes) and selected searches near large numbers to suggest conjectural values of G(3), etc. Computation complements analytic bounds and can suggest which values are 'arithmetical flukes'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite-exception results vs absolute bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Proving that only finitely many exceptions require many summands (e.g., only finitely many numbers need 9 cubes) is distinct from proving a uniform bound valid for all n; both are meaningful but different types of conclusions (G(k) vs g(k)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Landau's theorem that only finitely many numbers need 9 cubes is an example: such finite-exception theorems are weaker than establishing a global g(k), but yield important structural information about exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application to related hard problems (e.g., Goldbach)
rubrics_metrics.description: The circle method and analogous analytic apparatus can be applied (in principle) to additive prime problems; with additional hypotheses (e.g., generalized Riemann hypothesis) one can obtain near-Goldbach conclusions like 'every sufficiently large odd integer is sum of three primes'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hardy warns that solving prime-additive problems requires deeper prime-distribution inputs; conditional results assuming RH-type statements are achievable and are meaningful intermediate milestones.
